item.title: Syria’s central bank issues first letter of credit in 14 years
item.dc:creator: Pramod Kumar
item.description: Syria’s central bank has issued its first letter of credit in nearly 14 years, allowing local companies to trade internationally. The state-run Syrian Petroleum Company used the letter, issued on October 11, to import petroleum products from Aramco Trading, a subsidiary of Saudi Aramco, the state-owned Sana news agency reported. A letter of credit guarantees […]
item.content:encoded:
Syria’s central bank has issued its first letter of credit in nearly 14 years, allowing local companies to trade internationally.

The state-run Syrian Petroleum Company used the letter, issued on October 11, to import petroleum products from Aramco Trading, a subsidiary of Saudi Aramco, the state-owned Sana news agency reported.

A letter of credit guarantees payment to the seller through the importer’s bank, reducing risk for both parties.

The transaction marks a return to formal trade finance after years of reliance on informal arrangements and intermediaries in third countries, said Abdul Rahman Mohammed, a professor of finance and banking at the University of Hama.

The European Union and US lifted sanctions on Syria last year, following the ousting of leader Bashar Al Assad at the end of 2024. GCC companies have since announced major investments in the war-torn nation.

Syria’s banking sector reconnected with the international financial system in February after the central bank met US anti-money-laundering and counter-terrorism-financing requirements.

Last month Hamid Saif Alzaabi, president of the Middle East and North Africa Financial Action Task Force, told AGBI that Syria’s return to global finance had drawn renewed international scrutiny of its efforts to combat money laundering and illicit flows.

item.title: Acwa to consider solar and wind projects in Mongolia
item.dc:creator: Pramod Kumar
item.description: Saudi renewable energy company Acwa has signed a memorandum of cooperation with Mongolia’s Sun Steppe Power (SSP) to explore the cross-border export of electricity to China. The companies will assess building cross-border solar and wind power projects with a targeted capacity of 4.5 gigawatts, supported by a 500-megawatt-hour battery energy storage system, the state-run Saudi […]
item.content:encoded:
Saudi renewable energy company Acwa has signed a memorandum of cooperation with Mongolia’s Sun Steppe Power (SSP) to explore the cross-border export of electricity to China.

The companies will assess building cross-border solar and wind power projects with a targeted capacity of 4.5 gigawatts, supported by a 500-megawatt-hour battery energy storage system, the state-run Saudi Press Agency reported.

SSP is a subsidiary of London-listed Petro Matad, a hydrocarbon exploration and production company.

Acwa entered China’s renewables market in March 2025, signing agreements to develop more than 1GW of projects across several provinces.

The Public Investment Fund-controlled company aims to invest up to $30 billion in China by 2030.

Acwa executives also held discussions this week with Iraqi electricity minister Ali Saadi Waheeb about potentially doubling the capacity of a solar plant in Central Najaf governorate.

The company has 32 projects under development, with a combined power-generation capacity of 47GW and water desalination capacity of 2 million cubic metres per day.

Acwa’s shares, listed on the Saudi Exchange, closed at SAR160.10 on Wednesday and are down nearly 12 percent so far this year.

item.title: QatarEnergy reveals steep fall in profit and revenue
item.dc:creator: Pramod Kumar
item.description: QatarEnergy has reported a sharp decline in net profit and revenue in the first six months of 2026 due to the Iran conflict. An Iranian missile strike in March disrupted the state company’s liquefied natural gas export capacity. Net profit attributable plunged 69 percent to QAR15 billion ($4 billion) between January and June, compared to […]
item.content:encoded:
QatarEnergy has reported a sharp decline in net profit and revenue in the first six months of 2026 due to the Iran conflict.

An Iranian missile strike in March disrupted the state company’s liquefied natural gas export capacity.

Net profit attributable plunged 69 percent to QAR15 billion ($4 billion) between January and June, compared to QAR48 billion a year earlier, according to the company’s unaudited consolidated financial statement published on the UK Financial Conduct Authority data portal.

Revenue declined 35 percent to QAR87 billion in the first half.

Crude oil and condensate revenues dropped more than 55 percent and 29 percent, respectively. Income from LNG fell 5 percent, while natural gas declined 40 percent.

However, cash generated from operations rose to QAR21 billion between January and June, from QAR13 billion a year earlier. As a result, the company’s utilisation of own cash in financing activities increased by 500 percent, according to the financial statement.

As of June 30, total assets stood at QAR704 billion, while total liabilities reached QAR184 billion.

Following the Iranian strike on the Ras Laffan facility in March, QatarEnergy CEO Saad Al-Kaabi estimated annual revenue losses of $20 billion after the attacks disrupted nearly 17 percent of its export capacity.

Ras Laffan accounts for about 20 percent of global supply. It covers almost 30 percent of UAE gas demand through its Dolphin pipeline, a joint venture between Mubadala, Occidental Petroleum and TotalEnergies.

The Gulf state has warned that repairs could take up to five years.

The Qatari emir, Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad al-Thani, said this week that the US-Iran war had negatively affected the country’s public finances, leading to a sharp decline in revenue during the first half of 2026.

He confirmed that work on the North Field Gas expansion was progressing as planned, while the Golden Pass project in the US had made significant progress.

Further reading:

  • Qatar companies get grant to offset higher shipping costs
  • Fitch updates Qatar outlook on lower fears of LNG attacks
  • Qatar set to slip down LNG export rankings due to Iran war

item.title: Adia backs IPO of India’s Zetwerk as anchor investor
item.dc:creator: Pramod Kumar
item.description: Abu Dhabi Investment Authority (Adia) has joined as an anchor investor in the initial public offering (IPO) of Zetwerk, an industrial and consumer product manufacturer in India. The sovereign fund purchased 8.3 million shares or 5.55 percent of the IPO anchor book for INR1.2 billion ($13 million) through two investment vehicles, Zetwerk said. Zetwerk sold 149 […]
item.content:encoded:
Abu Dhabi Investment Authority (Adia) has joined as an anchor investor in the initial public offering (IPO) of Zetwerk, an industrial and consumer product manufacturer in India.

The sovereign fund purchased 8.3 million shares or 5.55 percent of the IPO anchor book for INR1.2 billion ($13 million) through two investment vehicles, Zetwerk said.

Zetwerk sold 149 million shares to 99 anchor investors at INR151, the upper end of the offer price band, generating INR22.5 billion.

The Indian technology-led manufacturing platform serves customers in utilities, renewable energy, artificial intelligence infrastructure, aerospace, space and defence, as well as the oil and gas sectors.

Zetwerk founders intend to use the IPO proceeds to repay debt.

Retail subscription will run from October 15-19 with a price band of INR143 to INR151 per share. The shares are expected to list on the Bombay and National Stock Exchanges, India’s two bourses, on October 23.

Last month Indian commerce and industry minister Piyush Goyal said the UAE was likely to significantly increase investment in India as the two nations raise bilateral trade to $200 billion by 2032.

Adia opened a new office in India’s free zone in October 2024 to accelerate its investment plans in the country.

The wealth fund backed the $2.3 billion IPO of the National Stock Exchange of India in September following its investment in the Indian government-backed National Investment and Infrastructure Fund.

Adia has anchored several IPOs in India, including the stockbroker Groww and the renewable energy company Clean Max Enviro Energy Solutions.

Further reading:

  • Adia invests in Indian spirits company Allied Blenders
  • UAE planning second $25bn India investment, minister says

item.title: Mubadala’s GlobalFoundries lands $21bn US chip project
item.dc:creator: Valentina Pasquali
item.description: Abu Dhabi-backed chipmaker GlobalFoundries will build and operate two semiconductor manufacturing plants, or fabs, at its site in New York state under a $21 billion joint US-Japan initiative. The US Commerce Department is separately receiving an equity stake of about 4 percent in the company, GlobalFoundries said in a press release on Wednesday. Japan will […]
item.content:encoded:
• Japan funds two new fabs
  • Washington’s stake rises to 7%
  • About 27,000 jobs to be created

Abu Dhabi-backed chipmaker GlobalFoundries will build and operate two semiconductor manufacturing plants, or fabs, at its site in New York state under a $21 billion joint US-Japan initiative.

The US Commerce Department is separately receiving an equity stake of about 4 percent in the company, GlobalFoundries said in a press release on Wednesday.

Japan will invest an initial $10 billion to build an already permitted 300mm fab by 2029. The 300mm wafer size is the standard for high-volume microchip production. A further $10 billion will fund the development of a new facility.

GlobalFoundries, which is majority-owned by UAE wealth fund Mubadala Investment Company, will contribute its technology and expertise to build and operate the plants.

“GF was selected because fabs of this scale require more than capital,” GlobalFoundries CEO Tim Breen said in a statement. “They require differentiated technology, operational excellence and a proven ability to execute.”

Each plant is projected to produce almost a million 300mm wafers a year at full capacity. Construction is expected to create about 27,000 direct and indirect jobs, with more than 1,000 highly skilled manufacturing roles also to be added.

Twenty 300mm fabs are expected to break ground globally in 2026 and 18 more next year, industry group SEMI said on Wednesday.

Further reading:

  • Mubadala’s GlobalFoundries lands $300m US award
  • Mubadala raises $2bn from GlobalFoundries share sale
  • GlobalFoundries commits $3bn to microchip research

Construction spending on this buildout is projected to jump 23 percent to $48 billion this year and 33 percent to $63 billion in 2027.

Japan’s funding of the GlobalFoundries plants is part of a trade deal with the US under which Japan pledged to invest $550 billion in the American economy in exchange for lower tariffs.

The US government’s new 4 percent stake in GlobalFoundries will bring its total holding to 7 percent, Reuters reported, citing Breen.

A Commerce Department award of nearly $1 billion to GlobalFoundries is also being amended to accelerate the chipmaker’s investment in the latest semiconductor technologies at its sites in Malta, New York, and Burlington, Vermont.

GlobalFoundries last week agreed a $2 billion deal with Taiwanese semiconductor manufacturer TSMC to build silicon interposers in the US. The components sit between AI processors and memory chips.

item.title: Qatar companies get grant to offset higher shipping costs
item.dc:creator: Pramod Kumar
item.description: The state-owned Qatar Development Bank (QDB) is supporting local manufacturers with a non-repayable grant to cover raw material shipping costs, which have soared due to the US-Iran war. The bank has increased its Logistics Support Fund to QAR400 million ($110 million) as part of its support package for Qatar’s industrial sector. The fund covers up […]
item.content:encoded:
The state-owned Qatar Development Bank (QDB) is supporting local manufacturers with a non-repayable grant to cover raw material shipping costs, which have soared due to the US-Iran war.

The bank has increased its Logistics Support Fund to QAR400 million ($110 million) as part of its support package for Qatar’s industrial sector.

The fund covers up to 80 percent of the increase in raw material shipping costs from pre-conflict levels for local manufacturers across all sectors, QDB said in a social media post.

The announcement comes a day after Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al-Thani said Qatar’s revenue dropped 42 percent while spending declined 14 percent in the first half of 2026.

Qatar has been among the mediators seeking a diplomatic end to the conflict and helped secure a temporary peace plan in June. However, the war has since widened to include fighting between Saudi Arabia and the Iran-backed Houthi militia.

CEO Abdulrahman Al-Sowaidi said the fund was expanded in response to private-sector feedback to help national manufacturers maintain production and offset rising costs for imported raw materials.

QDB has approved 436 applications under the fund, he said.

Local manufacturers can apply for the non-repayable grant more than once.

Last month, AGBI reported that supertanker freight rates from the Gulf to China now exceed $30 a barrel – nearly a third of the oil’s price – as the risk of crossing the Strait of Hormuz drives up costs.

In addition, war-risk cover was adding up to $8 to the cost of a barrel of oil because of the Iran war, according to David Osler, law and insurance editor at shipping news provider Lloyd’s List.

Further reading:

  • War hits Qatar’s public finances as revenue drops sharply
  • Why Iran gains more from an open, dangerous Hormuz
  • Gulf oil tankers earn $1m a day in ‘perfect storm’ of crises

item.title: US plans to ease sanctions on shadow fleet
item.dc:creator: Pramod Kumar
item.description: The US reportedly plans to ease sanctions on the shadow fleet transporting oil and petroleum products in an effort to ease record-high freight rates, sending crude prices lower on Thursday. Brent crude futures fell 1.5 percent to $104.50 a barrel by 03:00 GMT, while US West Texas Intermediate crude futures lost 1.2 percent to $94. […]
item.content:encoded:
• Brent crude falls 1.5% to $104
  • IEA says Gulf exports increasing
  • Houthis target eastern Saudi Arabia

The US reportedly plans to ease sanctions on the shadow fleet transporting oil and petroleum products in an effort to ease record-high freight rates, sending crude prices lower on Thursday.

Brent crude futures fell 1.5 percent to $104.50 a barrel by 03:00 GMT, while US West Texas Intermediate crude futures lost 1.2 percent to $94. Both benchmarks are up around 40 percent year-to-date.

The decline came despite intensifying attacks on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, an escalating conflict between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis in Yemen and fresh Iranian threats against US warships.

Record freight rates have hit demand for US crude, Reuters reported, citing energy secretary Chris Wright’s video address to the World Petroleum Congress in Riyadh.

US president Donald Trump has struck a diesel deal with Russia ahead of US midterm elections next month in an effort to cut fuel prices. Prices are more than 40 percent higher on average than a year ago, according to American Automobile Association data.

Saudi Arabia and the Houthi militia have continued to exchange retaliatory attacks.

A drone was intercepted and destroyed in eastern Saudi Arabia on Thursday morning, state news agency SPA reported.

Houthi militia spokesperson Yahya Saree said on social media on Thursday that the group had used an air-to-air missile to strike a Saudi Typhoon warplane that had taken off from Taif Air Base.

He added that Khalid International Airport in Riyadh had been hit again on Thursday.

The airport has been closed since attacks at the weekend, which followed a strike on an administrative building at Saudi Aramco headquarters.

Yemen has been divided for more than a decade between areas controlled by the UN-sanctioned government and those held by the Houthis. The country has suffered economic collapse and widespread poverty.

Further reading:

  • Two vessels sink off Oman as Hormuz attacks intensify
  • Russian shadow-fleet ship at risk of breaking up off Oman
  • Why Iran gains more from an open, dangerous Hormuz

Trump has said the Houthis were behaving “very badly” and warned that the US could join strikes on Yemen, despite having rejected Saudi Arabia’s previous requests.

Last week, the United Nations secretary-general’s special envoy for Yemen, Hans Grundberg, said the country had slid back into full-scale war.

“The conflict is intensifying, with Houthi offensives, attacks on Saudi infrastructure and threats to Red Sea shipping raising regional security and economic risks,” he said.

Elsewhere, Iran said it had acquired “significantly more advanced weapons”, although it had relied mainly on older-generation weapons in the early days of the conflict with the US and Israel, the state-run IRNA news agency reported.

The IRGC also threatened to sink US warships in the Strait of Hormuz, saying it was “counting the moments”, according to a report by the Tasnim agency.

Crude oil exports from GCC producers rose by more than 4 million barrels per day in September to about 75 percent of pre-war levels, according to the International Energy Agency.

However, Opec cut its forecast for 2026 global oil demand in its October report. It expects demand to grow next year, with stockpiles potentially being replenished.

The conflict in Yemen weighed on the Saudi stock exchange, which dropped 1.7 percent on Wednesday to a 43-month low.

Qatar’s main index slipped 0.7 percent, while Kuwait’s market gauge declined 1.4 percent.

Dubai and Abu Dhabi closed 0.6 percent and 0.4 percent higher, respectively.

item.title: Demand destruction: an indelicate forecast
item.dc:creator: James Drummond
item.description: Saudi oil minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman used this week’s WPC Energy Congress in Riyadh to reassure global markets of the kingdom’s commitment as a supplier of hydrocarbons and to find alternatives to export constraints in the Strait of Hormuz. As Francesca Washtell reported, Saudi Arabia plans to convert an unnamed gas pipeline to pump […]
item.content:encoded:
Saudi oil minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman used this week’s WPC Energy Congress in Riyadh to reassure global markets of the kingdom’s commitment as a supplier of hydrocarbons and to find alternatives to export constraints in the Strait of Hormuz.

As Francesca Washtell reported, Saudi Arabia plans to convert an unnamed gas pipeline to pump oil until May next year, which should add an incremental 1.2 million barrels per day to export capacity. Along with upgrades to the East-West pipeline, this could increase capacity to 10 million bpd over the next two to three years.

At the same event, Opec secretary-general Haitham Al Ghais projected that the global call for oil will rise by 1.7 million bpd next year as demand deferred by the US-Iran conflict returns.

Let us hope so.

Det Norske Veritas (DNV), a Norwegian organisation that examines energy supply and infrastructure worldwide, has produced its useful annual energy transition outlook. Demand features prominently.

DNV shares the view of the International Energy Agency, the watchdog whose analysis has long been more pessimistic than Opec’s. It estimates that global oil demand fell by 5.3 million bpd year on year in the second quarter of this year and by 3.4 million bpd in the third. Bear in mind that until February global oil demand was about 105 million bpd.

DNV, which is profit-making although owned by a Norwegian non-profit, also sets out a base scenario in which oil demand declines by 1.9 percent for the full year 2026. Most of the lost demand is recovered next year, when demand grows by 2.5 percent. That is roughly in line with Opec’s analysis.

The document becomes interesting – and, for us here in the Arabian Gulf, disturbing – when it considers a longer-term conflict.

Demand destruction is a phrase that haunts oil and gas producers such as Saudi Arabia. It speaks of unsold barrels that disappear permanently from end-users’ shopping lists as they turn to alternatives such as wind, solar, hydrogen and – whisper it quietly – coal.

DNV’s scenario assumes that the Middle East conflict persists until 2030 and that oil and gas prices remain elevated for those four years.

In that four-year conflict – by no means unthinkable – DNV sees demand destruction becoming structural. It draws parallels with the oil demand shocks of 1973 and 1979 and, in the gas market, Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

Shipping and aviation are relatively immune because alternative fuels are scarce to non-existent. Road transport and chemical feedstocks, however, are exposed, DNV says.

“Petrochemicals appear to be experiencing the largest demand reduction, with both oil and gas consumption declining by about 7 percent in 2026. Most of this decrease is in China,” the outlook says. China has considerable expertise in using coal as an alternative feedstock.

DNV foresees a short-term reduction in global oil and gas demand of 4-6 percent while a conflict lasts, and permanent demand destruction of 2-5 percent relative to its base case.

Such projections are necessarily hypothetical, with a wide margin of error. For Middle Eastern oil producers, the numbers are arguably painful but not catastrophic. They are, however, thought-provoking.

Separately, DNV downgraded its projections for carbon capture and storage, a technology on which hopes of limiting emissions rest. “Deployment over the last year has been progressing more slowly than anticipated,” the outlook says.

While the near-term project pipeline supports significant growth in carbon capture, final investment decisions have not been made at the pace previously assumed and several projects have been delayed, the study says.

Further reading

  • IEA slashes global oil demand forecast as war drives up prices
  • Bullish Opec says annual $700bn needed to meet oil demand
  • The Gulf needs carbon taxes, not just capture, to reach net zero

item.title: State spending cushions Gulf projects from war
item.dc:creator: Josh Corder
item.description: Gulf project awards edged higher year on year in the first nine months of 2026 despite the US-Iran war, as governments intervened to sustain energy and transport spending. GCC countries awarded contracts worth just over $200 billion between January and September, up 2.5 percent from a year earlier, Kamco Invest said in a quarterly update […]
item.content:encoded:
• Contract awards rise 2.5% annually
  • Energy major factor with gas up 60%
  • Double-digit declines in third quarter

Gulf project awards edged higher year on year in the first nine months of 2026 despite the US-Iran war, as governments intervened to sustain energy and transport spending.

GCC countries awarded contracts worth just over $200 billion between January and September, up 2.5 percent from a year earlier, Kamco Invest said in a quarterly update drawing on data from MEED Projects.

Energy carried much of the spending. Gas awards rose about 60 percent year on year in the third quarter, and Saudi Aramco signed more than $12 billion of upstream contracts, mostly at the start of the year.

The UAE pressed ahead with Dubai’s $9 billion Gold Line metro and Etihad Rail through the summer, AGBI reported in August. Energy minister Suhail Al Mazrouei said Abu Dhabi was pushing on with $57 billion of infrastructure across 500 projects.

In Saudi Arabia, contractor awards jumped 82 percent year on year in the first half, Saudi Contractors Authority platform Scavo said in September. The kingdom awarded more than $24 billion in the third quarter, half the Gulf total.

But the third quarter alone told a harsher story. Awards between July and September fell by more than a third year on year to just over $47 billion across the region, and by about a fifth compared with the second quarter.

Oman suffered the steepest decline in project awards across the Gulf in the third quarter. New contract awards in the sultanate plunged almost 97 percent year on year, to just $76 million from more than $2 billion. A single gas-facilities contract that Petroleum Development Oman signed with Egypt’s Enppi in June was worth almost five times that total.

Further reading:

  • UAE presses on with mega-projects to reassure investors
  • Saudi construction jumps despite PIF taking a back seat
  • Abu Dhabi plans construction rush after quitting Opec

Every other GCC country also posted a double-digit fall year on year in the third quarter. Bahrain’s awards fell by more than two-thirds and Qatar’s by almost two-thirds. Kuwait’s more than halved, while the UAE’s dropped by about a quarter.

Kamco blamed the slowdown on disrupted energy exports and trade routes, as well as attacks on energy infrastructure. It said the disruption would hit Gulf states’ ability “to fund and award planned 2026 contracts”.

item.title: Two vessels sink off Oman as Hormuz attacks intensify
item.dc:creator: John Crowley
item.description: A bulk carrier and a container vessel attacked close to the Strait of Hormuz sank off Oman on Wednesday, according to shipping industry sources. The incidents mark a further escalation in strikes on commercial shipping. At least 28 vessels have been targeted around the chokepoint since September 28, the highest frequency of attacks since the […]
item.content:encoded:
• Container ship is latest attacked
  • All crew safely evacuated
  • Bulk carrier was being salvaged

A bulk carrier and a container vessel attacked close to the Strait of Hormuz sank off Oman on Wednesday, according to shipping industry sources.

The incidents mark a further escalation in strikes on commercial shipping. At least 28 vessels have been targeted around the chokepoint since September 28, the highest frequency of attacks since the conflict began in February.

The Antigua and Barbuda-flagged Cape Dao, a bulk carrier, began sinking on October 13, following an attack on September 23 that led to the death of one crew member and forced the evacuation of 26 others.

Photographs supplied to AGBI by shipping sources show extensive fire damage to the ship’s superstructure, with large sections blackened by the blaze.

The vessel was struck three weeks ago by two unidentified projectiles about 15 nautical miles northeast of Khasab, Oman, damaging its engine room and causing an onboard fire, industry sources said.

The blaze was extinguished the following day and the ship was being towed towards a dry dock in Oman.

However, a navigation warning issued on Tuesday indicated that its condition had deteriorated significantly. A maritime notice on Wednesday said the vessel had sunk.

Arsenio Longo, founder of maritime intelligence company Huax, said the sequence of events “raised questions around the difficulties of stabilising and recovering heavily damaged commercial vessels under present security conditions”.

Pakistan’s National Hydrographic Office, which monitors maritime activities in Middle Eastern waters, said both ships had gone down, according to The Wall Street Journal.

President Donald Trump’s pledge not to attack Iran before next month’s midterm elections in the US has given Tehran a window to harass Gulf shipping while preparing for possible renewed strikes, regional analysts have told AGBI.

“The midterm deadline has given Tehran greater room for manoeuvre,” said Neil Quilliam, a Middle East specialist at the Chatham House think tank and AGBI columnist. Quilliam added that the Iranian leadership was likely to calibrate its actions to avoid provoking an escalation.

Container ship sinks after fresh strike

In a separate incident, the Singapore-flagged container ship GFS Pride was struck by an unidentified projectile on October 13, about one nautical mile east of Ras Makhbuq, Oman.

The impact caused damage and an onboard fire, with a navigation warning on Wednesday reporting that the vessel was adrift.

Pictures and video supplied to AGBI show sections of the vessel protruding above the water on Tuesday with shipping containers floating nearby.

A maritime notice on Wednesday confirmed that the vessel had sunk. Singapore’s Maritime and Port Authority said all 21 crew members had been safely evacuated.

Longo said the sinkings raised environmental questions, although there was no evidence of a significant oil release.

“Both incidents underline concerns about the fuel and other substances remaining aboard,” he said. “Even bulk carries and containers ships can carry considerable quantities of bunker fuel and lubricating oil.

”Depending on where the damage occurred and whether the fuel tanks remained intact, a sinking could result in pollution that may be difficult to contain, particularly if the wreck is in deeper water.”

Further reading:

  • Why Iran gains more from an open, dangerous Hormuz
  • Gulf suppliers urged to halt Hormuz crossings
  • Frank Kane: Who is winning the Battle of Hormuz?
